historical_timeline.summary: Born into slavery on the Burroughs plantation, Franklin County, Virginia; the exact date is uncertain.
Emancipated; moved with his family to Malden, West Virginia.
Beaten in New York City; head lacerations and a torn ear.

Historical clinicopathological conference attributes his death to malignant hypertension with kidney failure.

claims.statement: Booker T. Washington was born into slavery on the James Burroughs plantation in Franklin County, Virginia, in 1856; the National Park Service timeline gives the date as April 5, 1856.

Washington wrote in Up from Slavery (1901) that he was not sure of the exact date of his birth and estimated the year as 1858 or 1859; the April 5, 1856 date traces to a report by his brother John after his death and was adopted by the Tuskegee trustees.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The exact birth date is uncertain; the case uses the NPS date of April 5, 1856.

claims.statement: After emancipation in 1865 Washington moved with his mother, Jane, and his family to Malden, West Virginia, where he worked in the salt and coal mines; a National Park Service release gives his mother's death as 1876.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The source gives no cause of death; other accounts give 1874.

claims.statement: Washington opened Tuskegee Institute in Tuskegee, Alabama, on July 4, 1881, at age 25, and led it for the rest of his life; in March 1915 he sponsored National Negro Health Week.

In 1911 Washington was beaten in New York City and received two large gashes in his head and a torn ear, recovering without apparent sequelae; he had chronic indigestion, especially when traveling, and spent several days in 1911 at the Battle Creek Sanitarium.
claims.clinical_interpretation: From the annotated hospital record published with the 2006 clinicopathological conference.

claims.statement: When Washington was admitted to the Rockefeller Institute hospital on November 2, 1915, his blood pressure was 220/150. He reported palpitations two weeks earlier, tiring quickly, frontal headaches one or two days out of every eight or nine, and slower thinking; the record also notes weight loss, failing vision, frequent urination, and avid thirst.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented anchor for the synthetic hypertension and kidney disease episode.

claims.statement: In early November 1915, after several months of failing health, Dr. W. A. Bastedo in New York diagnosed Bright's disease, a contemporary term for kidney disease; Dr. Lucas G. Cole at the Rockefeller Institute hospital agreed, and Washington was moved to St. Luke's Hospital.

Washington traveled home from New York and died at Tuskegee on November 14, 1915, at age 59; the New York Times reported hardening of the arteries as the cause, and the National Park Service attributes his death to conditions related to high blood pressure.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without graphic detail.

claims.statement: A 2006 historical clinicopathological conference at the University of Maryland School of Medicine reviewed his hospital record and concluded that he presented with malignant hypertension that caused kidney failure.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective diagnosis; the modern problem list uses hypertensive kidney disease without asserting it as historical fact.

claims.statement: A 1915 remark by Dr. Bastedo attributing the death partly to 'racial characteristics' was read by Washington's Chicago physician, Dr. George C. Hall, as implying syphilis; the hospital Wassermann test was negative, and the 2006 review did not support that explanation.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Teaching point about biased attribution in medical records; do not repeat the remark without this context.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Washington returns one week after starting amlodipine and losartan for severe hypertension with stage G3b chronic kidney disease. His home readings, taken twice daily, have fallen from above 200 systolic to the 160s and 170s over 100s. He has had one mild frontal headache this week, fewer than before, and no chest pain, breathlessness, weakness, confusion, or sudden change in vision. His palpitations are less frequent. He has had no lightheadedness on standing and no ankle swelling, and he takes both medicines every morning. His reading vision is still blurred and he still gets up twice a night to urinate. He asks how to keep to the plan on travel days. His nephrology consultation, kidney ultrasound, and echocardiogram were done today.

referral.question: Severe hypertension with chronic kidney disease stage G3b and severely increased albuminuria in a 59-year-old man. Please assess the cause of the kidney disease, advise on kidney-protective therapy and blood pressure targets, and share his long-term care
referral.urgency: Soon, within one week; kidney ultrasound and echocardiogram booked for the morning of the consultation
referral.pertinent_history: Frontal headaches every week or so, palpitations, fatigue, slower concentration, blurred reading vision, and nocturia. Blood pressure 212/128 mmHg with no chest pain, breathlessness, or focal neurologic deficit; dilated funduscopy shows arteriolar narrowing and arteriovenous nicking without hemorrhages, exudates, or papilledema, and the ECG shows sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage, so we are treating as an outpatient. Creatinine 2.1 mg/dL (eGFR 36), BUN 34 mg/dL, potassium 4.4 and bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, urine albumin-creatinine ratio 820 mg/g, calcium 9.1 and phosphate 4.2 mg/dL, PTH 92 pg/mL, hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL with ferritin 210 ng/mL and transferrin saturation 26 percent, HbA1c 5.4 percent, LDL cholesterol 138 mg/dL. No earlier creatinine is on file. Never smoker; he travels often for work. Started today: amlodipine 10 mg and losartan 50 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg daily
questions: Is this hypertensive nephrosclerosis, or does anything point to another kidney disease or a secondary cause of hypertension that needs testing?
Do you agree with titrating losartan to the maximum dose and adding an SGLT2 inhibitor, and how much rise in creatinine should we accept?
What blood pressure target should we aim for, and which agent should come next if he stays above it?
Do his bicarbonate, PTH, and hemoglobin need treatment now?
How often should we monitor, and when should he return to nephrology?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Washington is seen at the request of Dr. Whitfield one week after presenting with headaches, palpitations, fatigue, and a blood pressure of 212/128 mmHg. On amlodipine and losartan his home readings have fallen to the 160s and 170s over 100s, he has had one mild headache this week, and his palpitations are less frequent. He has had no chest pain, breathlessness, weakness, confusion, or sudden change in vision, and no lightheadedness on standing or ankle swelling. He gets up twice a night to urinate and has seen no blood in the urine. He takes no NSAIDs or other over-the-counter products. He travels often for work and wants a plan that he can keep on the road
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Today's kidney ultrasound: both kidneys small (9.4 and 9.6 cm) and echogenic, symmetric, without hydronephrosis. Today's echocardiogram: concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, ejection fraction 60 percent. Last week's ECG and dilated funduscopic examination. Both basic metabolic panels, the urine albumin-creatinine ratio, mineral studies, blood count, and iron studies. No urinalysis with microscopy is on file

assessment.display: Chronic kidney disease stage G3b A3
assessment.assessment: Small, echogenic, symmetric kidneys with severe hypertension, left ventricular hypertrophy, and hypertensive retinopathy fit long-standing hypertensive nephrosclerosis, and the disease is chronic, not acute. Albuminuria of 820 mg/g is high for nephrosclerosis alone, so the response to treatment is the test: a fall of at least 30 percent supports the diagnosis. One week after losartan, creatinine is 2.2 mg/dL (up 5 percent), eGFR 34, and potassium 4.6 mmol/L, so blockade can be pushed further. His risk of progression is very high

assessment.display: Severe hypertension with hypertensive kidney disease
assessment.assessment: 172/104 mmHg, improving but far above target. The symmetric kidneys, the absence of an abdominal bruit, and the small creatinine rise on losartan argue against renal artery stenosis, and his potassium is normal. Secondary causes need testing only if blood pressure stays above target on three agents including a diuretic

assessment.display: Mild anemia of chronic kidney disease
assessment.assessment: Hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL with ferritin 210 ng/mL and transferrin saturation 26 percent: iron replete, and well above any threshold for treatment

assessment.display: Mineral and bone disorder and acid-base status of chronic kidney disease
assessment.assessment: PTH 92 pg/mL is mildly raised with normal calcium and phosphate, and bicarbonate 21 to 22 mmol/L is above the level that needs alkali. Neither needs treatment now

recommendations: Increase losartan to 100 mg daily today and continue amlodipine 10 mg daily
Start dapagliflozin 10 mg daily today: eGFR is above 20 and albuminuria above 200 mg/g. It is for kidney protection, so continue it even if eGFR later falls below 20
Accept a creatinine rise of up to 30 percent from 2.1 mg/dL after these changes; check potassium and creatinine in about three weeks
If blood pressure is still above target on full doses of losartan and amlodipine, add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg daily, which works at his level of kidney function
Target a standardized office systolic pressure below 120 mmHg if tolerated, with below 130/80 as the first step
Avoid NSAIDs; sick-day rule to hold losartan, dapagliflozin, and any diuretic on days with vomiting, diarrhea, or poor fluid intake
Sodium below 2 g a day, with a plan for meals while traveling

Urine albumin-creatinine ratio once the regimen is complete. Urinalysis with microscopy and further testing for other kidney diseases if albuminuria does not fall on treatment or kidney function changes unexpectedly
Calcium, phosphate, PTH, and a baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D at about six months; hemoglobin at least yearly. No alkali, vitamin D analog, or iron now
Pneumococcal and hepatitis B vaccination for chronic kidney disease
Calculate the kidney failure risk once eGFR has settled on full therapy
